issues.title: Missing induced-lattice covolume in the parameter count

failure_location.quote: The volume of $D_0$ approximates the number of integer points it contains.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the intrinsic volume of D0 itself approximates its integer-point count. From eq:D0_def and the decimation matrix, for prime N the integer points form the lattice generated by e_i-e_N; its Gram determinant is N and its covolume is sqrt(N). Thus the leading lattice-point count is vol(D0)/sqrt(N), up to boundary error, rather than vol(D0). The same induced-lattice density enters the affine Dgamma count, so the omitted factor is material to the subsequent rho and beta2 estimates.
issues.overall_effect: The explicit estimates for the numbers of candidate coefficient vectors, and hence the derived beta2 parameter formula, have an unaccounted N-dependent normalization. The uniqueness and dynamic-programming results are unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Let S be the real nullspace imposed by the decimation constraints and let Λ=S∩Z^N. Compute its intrinsic covolume Δ_N from an integer lattice basis. Replace each approximation |D^Z|≈vol_S(D) for D_0 and the nonempty affine sets D_γ by |D^Z|≈vol_S(D)/Δ_N, up to boundary error; for prime N, Δ_N=√N. Propagate the factor Δ_N^−1 through the formulas for ρ and the resulting β_2 estimate, and update the associated numerical parameter estimates.
issues.why_classification: This is an incorrect lattice-density inference rather than a transcription error. A complete repair requires a contained but nontrivial covolume calculation and quantitative rederivation of the ρ and β_2 estimates. The repair is localized to the parameter analysis and preserves its architecture and the inversion results, so it is moderate rather than serious.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Moreover, the LLL method depends on several parameters, and a study of their optimal selection would be valuable for practical applications.

issues.title: Strict Dgamma ball excludes the desired boundary vector

failure_location.quote: We again define the integer points in $D_\gamma$ as $D_{\gamma}^\mathbb{Z}=D_{\gamma}\cap\mathbb{Z}^N$, which contains the set of valid coefficient vectors ${\bm \alpha}$ for the given $\gamma$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that Dgamma's integer points contain the valid coefficient vectors. The old definition instead requires ||alpha-gamma xbar||_2<K. For gamma=1, eq:x_star identifies alpha=x as the desired vector, the decimation constraints hold exactly, and ||x-xbar||_2=K, so this required vector lies on the excluded boundary. Consequently the subsequent probabilistic count can omit a vector that the source itself says must contribute to rho(beta2,1).
issues.overall_effect: The candidate domain used in the beta2 count does not contain the guaranteed desired vectors at gamma=±1, so the rho bookkeeping and its interpretation require a boundary correction. Other sections are unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the strict condition ||α−γx̄||_2<K in D_γ by the non-strict condition ||α−γx̄||_2≤K. For γ=±1, separate α=γx as a deterministic unit contribution to ρ before applying the random-sum approximation to the remaining lattice points, where ||α−γx||_1 is nonzero. The continuous volume and asymptotic scaling estimates for the remaining points are unchanged.
issues.why_classification: Although the comparison-symbol correction is forced by the preceding bound, the probabilistic bookkeeping relies on the defective open domain and must treat the exact boundary vector separately. That is a short, routine boundary case with no new lemma, method change, or rate loss, making the issue minor rather than a mere typo or a moderate defect.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Moreover, the LLL method depends on several parameters, and a study of their optimal selection would be valuable for practical applications.

issues.title: Coefficient-weighted error in the full truncated lattice vector

failure_location.quote: Since the correct ${\bf b}$ lies within $1/\beta_3$ of ${\bf x}^*$, rounding succeeds for sufficiently large $\beta_3$ values.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims a uniform 1/beta3 perturbation bound for the whole correct lattice vector. If C=floor(beta3 B), z=[x;1], b=Cz/beta3, and x*=Bz, then b-x*=(C-beta3 B)z/beta3. Each coordinate is therefore bounded in general by ||z||_1/beta3, not by 1/beta3. For the first N identity-block coordinates, the reported integral beta3 makes the identity columns exact and a separate 1/beta3 bound can be obtained; that special block argument, rather than the asserted global bound, is what can justify signal rounding.
issues.overall_effect: The old source does not establish the claimed global perturbation control for the truncated lattice vector. A properly projected top-block rounding step may still be valid, so this defect alone does not invalidate the reported reconstructions.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Withdraw the claimed global 1/β_3 perturbation bound. In general, for z=[x;1], state the coordinatewise bound ||(⌊β_3B⌋/β_3−B)z||_∞≤||z||_1/β_3. For integral β_3, as used in the experiments, let P_A select the first N coordinates and note that the scaled identity columns are exact, so ||P_A(b−x*)||_∞<1/β_3; justify signal rounding only from this projected bound.
issues.why_classification: The old statement uses an invalid coefficient-independent truncation inference, so it is not a typo. The needed matrix calculation is short and local, and the stronger bound on the only coordinates used for signal extraction preserves the rounding method and reconstruction conclusion without meaningful loss.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Motivated by the overall limitations of these ILP results, we employed a reformulation of \cref{eq:ip_better} as a lattice reduction problem, as described in \cite{levinson2023}.

issues.title: Exact beta0 check is incompatible with a generic truncation scale
issues.failure_explanation: In the B0 row, the scaled-and-truncated last basis entry is floor(beta3 beta0). Hence a lattice vector with gamma=±1 has rescaled coordinate b_N=±floor(beta3 beta0)/beta3. The algorithm instead tests the exact equality b_N=±beta0 and states no compatibility condition on its beta3 input. Unless beta3 beta0 is integral, even a correct reduced-basis vector fails this test; with beta0=0.1 there are arbitrarily large integer scales not divisible by 10 for which this occurs.
issues.overall_effect: The generic pseudocode may fail to return a valid candidate solely because of its scale choice. The reported choice beta0=0.1 and beta3=100 is compatible, so this does not by itself invalidate the reported numerical runs.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Set q=⌊β_3β_0⌋, require q≥1, and test the integer reduced-basis coordinate against ±q, or equivalently test the rescaled coordinate b_N against ±q/β_3. This exactly recognizes γ=±1 for every permitted truncation scale and retains the reported choice β_0=0.1, β_3=100.
issues.why_classification: The generic pseudocode uses the untruncated value in a test that must reflect the truncated basis. Correcting that local marker test, with the routine nonzero-marker condition, preserves the algorithm, output guarantee, and reported experiments. It is a genuine algorithmic defect but needs no nontrivial new argument.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Motivated by the overall limitations of these ILP results, we employed a reformulation of \cref{eq:ip_better} as a lattice reduction problem, as described in \cite{levinson2023}.

issues.title: Ambient LLL vector is not projected before signal extraction

failure_location.quote: \State ${\bf y} \gets \pm{\bf b} + \overline{\bf x}$ rounded entrywise to integers

issues.failure_explanation: By eq:lattice_basis, b is an ambient lattice vector containing the N-coordinate A block, the B0 coordinate, and all B1 and B2 constraint coordinates. The instruction adds this full vector to the N-vector xbar, which is undefined. Moreover, the required sign is determined by b_N=gamma beta0: for gamma=1 the A block is added, while for gamma=-1 it must be negated.
issues.overall_effect: Taken literally, the candidate-extraction line cannot execute and does not define which integer signal is tested. The intended implementation is recoverable from the surrounding block notation.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Let P_A select the first N coordinates of the ambient lattice vector. Replace the extraction line by y=round(sP_A b+x̄), where s=1 when the B_0 marker identifies γ=1 and s=−1 when it identifies γ=−1; equivalently, for positive β_0, use the sign of the correctly scaled B_0 coordinate. No constraint-block coordinates should enter y.
issues.why_classification: The displayed block decomposition and the B_0 marker uniquely determine both the required projection and sign. Adding the full ambient vector to x̄ is ill-typed, and the source itself forces the corrected object without changing any inference, construction, or guarantee. This is therefore a transcriptional defect.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Motivated by the overall limitations of these ILP results, we employed a reformulation of \cref{eq:ip_better} as a lattice reduction problem, as described in \cite{levinson2023}.

issues.title: Expected guess error used in a universal runtime claim

failure_location.quote: This gives a pseudo-polynomial upper bound on the runtime of any iteration of \Cref{alg:memo_1D} or \Cref{alg:memo_2D} in terms of the current subproblem size $N$, number of coefficients $M$, and integer bounds $L$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims a pseudo-polynomial upper bound applying to any iteration. The displayed derivation's final step invokes eq:K_bound, which only bounds the expectation of K under the binomial model and does not bound a worst-case realized input. Thus the written argument supports at most a heuristic or average-scale substitution, not the stated universal bound. Because xbar is obtained by orthogonally retaining selected Fourier modes, the old definitions do permit the separate deterministic estimate K≤||x||_2≤sqrt(N)L, but that is not the bound the derivation invokes.
issues.overall_effect: The stated runtime order is not justified by the argument as written, although it can be recovered without changing the asymptotic order. No inversion theorem or algorithmic construction is lost.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the use of E[K] in the worst-case runtime derivation by the deterministic estimate K=||(I−P_F)x||_2≤||x||_2≤√N L, where P_F is the orthogonal projection onto the retained Fourier modes and x̄=P_Fx. Substituting this bound into the estimate for log B recovers the same O(N^7 log^2(MNL)) per-iteration runtime order.
issues.why_classification: Using an expectation to justify a universal bound is an invalid inference, so the issue is substantive rather than typographical. A single routine projection-norm estimate already available from the old definitions restores the universal claim with the same asymptotic rate and no change to either algorithm.

issues.title: Factor-of-two error in the 11-by-13 sampling percentage

failure_location.quote: the $11 \times 13$ matrix required $8 / 143 \approx 5.6\%$ of DFT coefficients for reliable inversion.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that reliable 11-by-13 inversion used 8 of 143 DFT coefficients, or 5.6%. The old tab:rect actually reports 16 coefficients for the successful M=5 row. Thus the supported percentage is 16/143≈11.2%, not 5.6%; this exceeds 350/3600≈9.7%, rather than being smaller as the following prose claims.
issues.overall_effect: The recovery result itself remains reported, but the measurement percentage and the claimed advantage over the 60-by-60 case are wrong.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the successful 11×13 measurement count to 16/143≈11.2%, as reported by the M=5 row of the table. Replace the subsequent comparison accordingly: 11.2% is greater than 350/3600≈9.7%, so the claimed percentage advantage over the 60×60 case must be removed or reversed. Retain the reported successful recovery itself.
issues.why_classification: The table supports the recovery experiment but not the claimed 5.6% sampling rate or its asserted advantage. Correcting the numbers withdraws a coherent empirical efficiency claim, so this is not a typo or a same-guarantee minor repair. The loss is limited to one comparison and requires no reconstruction of the method, making the issue moderate.
